text.b: Parsing Two-Column Papers Without Crossing the Gutter

page.text: A. Author, B. Author and C. Author
Two-column scientific layouts are common in engineering and life-science publishing, and naive
text extraction walks straight across the gutter. This synthetic manuscript exercises a parser
on a controllable layout: spanning title, spanning abstract, two body columns, a full-width
table, a numbered display equation, a figure caption and a reference list. The intended reading
order is column-major inside each band and top-to-bottom across bands. Margins carry a running
banner and a folio that must never reach the body text.
Reading order is a property of the layout,
not of the content stream. A parser that
sorts glyphs by their y coordinate alone
will interleave the left and right columns
line by line, producing sentences that
alternate between two unrelated paragraphs.
Sorting by x first is equally wrong, because
it destroys the vertical flow inside a
column. The correct model cuts the page into
bands at spanning elements and then reads
each column of a band from top to bottom.
Table reconstruction needs cell geometry
rather than whitespace heuristics. When a
tabular block is drawn without ruling lines,
the only reliable signal is the alignment of
cell boxes across rows, combined with the
vertical gaps between cells inside a row.
Column anchors derived from those boxes let
a grid be rebuilt as Markdown, which is what
downstream parameter extraction expects.

Equations are detected before prose
assembly, because their glyph runs are
interleaved with superscripts and subscripts
that would otherwise fragment a paragraph.
LaTeX math fonts are a strong signal, and
the equation number at the right margin
confirms the block. The raw text is joined
in reading order without rewriting the
mathematics.
